question: During an OSCE instrument station, you are shown a curved, blunt-ended instrument with a cup-shaped tip used in middle ear surgery under the operating microscope. Which instrument is this most likely to be?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Jobson Horne probe has a ring-ended (cerumen loop) tip and a pointed end, used for ear wax removal and minor ear procedures in the outpatient setting — not under the operating microscope for middle ear surgery.

Hartmann's forceps are slender alligator-type grasping forceps used for foreign body removal from the external auditory canal and outpatient ear procedures. They are not the blunt cup-tipped instrument used for ossicular manipulation in the middle ear.

answers.text: Wullstein middle ear instrument (cup-ended micro-ossicular forceps / Duckbill elevator)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Wullstein-type cup-ended micro-instruments — including the duckbill elevator and micro-cup forceps — are specifically designed for middle ear surgery under the operating microscope. Their blunt, cup-shaped tips allow manipulation of the ossicular chain and tympanic membrane remnants without causing inadvertent injury to delicate middle ear structures.

Tilley's forceps are long, angled nasal forceps used for nasal dressing changes, nasal packing, and foreign body removal from the nasal cavity — entirely the wrong anatomical region and purpose for the instrument described.

overallFeedback.feedback: In ENT instrument identification, match the physical design to the anatomical region and procedure: middle ear microsurgery = Wullstein cup-ended instruments; nasal = Tilley's; ear canal outpatient = Hartmann's or Jobson Horne.

Well done. Middle ear microsurgery requires Wullstein-type micro-instruments. Matching the instrument's design (blunt cup tip) to its function (ossicular manipulation under microscope) is the OSCE technique.
